In [[computer science]], the '''Hunt–Szymanski algorithm''',<ref>{{cite web |url=https://imada.sdu.dk/~rolf/Edu/DM823/E16/HuntSzymanski.pdf |title=The Hunt-Szymanski Algorithm for LCS |date=January 12, 2017 |publisher=Department of Mathematics and Computer Science, University of Southern Denmark }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=New tabulation and sparse dynamic programming based techniques for sequence similarity problems |author=Grabowski, Szymon |journal=Discrete Applied Mathematics |pages=96–103 |volume=212 |number=C |year=2016|doi=10.1016/j.dam.2015.10.040 |s2cid=14005194 |issn=0166-218X|doi-access=free |arxiv=1312.2217 }}</ref> also known as '''Hunt–McIlroy algorithm''', is a solution to the [[longest common subsequence problem]]. It was one of the first non-heuristic algorithms used in [[diff]], which compares a pair of files, each represented as a sequence of lines. To this day, variations of this algorithm are found in incremental [[version control system]]s, [[wiki software|wiki engine]]s, and [[molecular phylogenetics]] research software.

The [[worst-case complexity]] for this algorithm is {{math|''O''(''n''<sup>2</sup> log ''n'')}}, but in practice {{math|''O''(''n'' log ''n'')}} is rather expected.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Bounds on the Complexity of the Longest Common Subsequence Problem |url=https://www.ics.uci.edu/~dan/pubs/p1-ullman.pdf |author1=Aho, A. |author2=Hirschberg, D. |author3=Ullman, J. |journal=Journal of the ACM |pages=1–12 |volume=23 |number=1 |year=1976 |doi=10.1145/321921.321922 |s2cid=10957346 |issn=0004-5411 }}</ref><ref>See Section 5.6 of [[Alfred Aho|Aho, A. V.]], [[J. E. Hopcroft|Hopcroft, J. E.]], [[Jeffrey Ullman|Ullman, J. D.]], ''Data Structures and Algorithms.'' Addison-Wesley, 1983. {{ISBN|0-201-00023-7}}</ref>

== History ==
The algorithm was proposed by [[Harold S. Stone]] as a generalization of a special case solved by Thomas G.&nbsp;Szymanski.<ref name="HM76"/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.ime.usp.br/~is/papir/sctp/node3.html |title=Sequence Comparison: Some Theory and Some Practice |author=Imre Simon |date=April 2, 1988 |location=Universidade de São Paulo }}</ref><ref>Szymanski, T. G. (1975) A special case of the maximal common subsequence problem. Technical Report TR-170, Computer Science Lab., Princeton University.</ref> [[James W.&nbsp;Hunt]] refined the idea, implemented the first version of the candidate-listing algorithm used by [[diff]] and embedded it into an older framework of [[Douglas McIlroy]].<ref name="HM76">{{cite journal |first1=James W. |last1=Hunt |first2=M. Douglas |last2=McIlroy |author2-link=Douglas McIlroy |title=An Algorithm for Differential File Comparison |volume=41 |journal=Computing Science Technical Report |publisher=Bell Laboratories |date=June 1976|url=http://www.cs.dartmouth.edu/~doug/diff.pdf}}</ref>

The description of the algorithm appeared as a technical report by Hunt and McIlroy in 1976.<ref name="HM76"/> The following year, a variant of the algorithm was finally published in a joint paper by Hunt and Szymanski.<ref name="HM76"/><ref>{{cite journal |author1=Hunt, James W. |author2=Szymanski, Thomas G. |title=A fast algorithm for computing longest common subsequences |url=http://www.cs.ust.hk/mjg_lib/bibs/DPSu/DPSu.Files/HuSz77.pdf |journal=[[Communications of the ACM]] |pages=350–353 |volume=20 |number=5 |year=1977 |doi=10.1145/359581.359603 |s2cid=3226080 |issn=0001-0782 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220322010324/https://cse.hkust.edu.hk/mjg_lib/bibs/DPSu/DPSu.Files/HuSz77.pdf |archive-date=2022-03-22 |url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Algorithm==
The Hunt–Szymanski algorithm is a modification to a basic solution for the longest common subsequence problem, which has complexity {{math|''O''(''n''<sup>2</sup>)}}. The solution is modified so that there are lower time and space requirements for the algorithm when it is working with typical inputs.

===Basic longest common subsequence solution===

====Algorithm====
Let {{math|''A<sub>i</sub>''}} be the {{math|''i''}}th element of the first sequence.

Let {{math|''B<sub>j</sub>''}} be the {{math|''j''}}th element of the second sequence.

Let {{math|''P<sub>ij</sub>''}} be the length of the longest common subsequence for the first {{math|''i''}} elements of {{math|''A''}} and the first {{math|''j''}} elements {{math|''B''}}.
<math display="block">
 P_{ij} =
 \begin{cases}
  0 & \text{if}\ i = 0\ \text{or}\ j = 0, \\
  1 + P_{i-1, j-1} & \text{if}\ A_i = B_j, \\
  \max(P_{i-1, j}, P_{i, j-1}) & \text{if}\ A_i \ne B_j.
 \end{cases}
</math>

====Example====
[[File:Longest Common Subsequence Recursion.png|thumb|A table showing the recursive steps that the basic longest common subsequence algorithm takes]]
Consider the sequences {{math|''A''}} and {{math|''B''}}.

{{math|''A''}} contains three elements:
<math display="block">
 \begin{align}
  A_1 = a, \\
  A_2 = b, \\
  A_3 = c.
\end{align}
</math>

{{math|''B''}} contains three elements:
<math display="block">
 \begin{align}
  B_1 = a, \\
  B_2 = c, \\
  B_3 = b.
 \end{align}
</math>

The steps that the above algorithm would perform to determine the length of the longest common subsequence for both sequences are shown in the diagram. The algorithm correctly reports that the longest common subsequence of the two sequences is two elements long.

====Complexity====
The above algorithm has worst-case time and space complexities of {{math|''O''(''mn'')}} (see [[big O notation]]), where {{math|''m''}} is the number of elements in sequence {{math|''A''}}, and {{math|''n''}} is the number of elements in sequence {{math|''B''}}. The Hunt–Szymanski algorithm modifies this algorithm to have a worst-case [[time complexity]] of {{math|''O''(''mn'' log ''m'')}} and [[space complexity]] of {{math|''O''(''mn'')}}, though it regularly beats the worst case with typical inputs.

===Essential matches===

===={{math|''k''}}-candidates====
The Hunt–Szymanski algorithm only considers what the authors call essential matches, or {{math|''k''}}-candidates. {{math|''k''}}-candidates are pairs of indices {{math|(''i'', ''j'')}} such that
<math display="block">
 \begin{align}
  A_i &= B_j, \\
  P_{ij} &> \max(P_{i-1, j}, P_{i, j-1}).
 \end{align}
</math>

The second point implies two properties of {{math|''k''}}-candidates:
* There is a common subsequence of length {{math|''k''}} in the first {{math|''i''}} elements of sequence {{math|''A''}} and the first {{math|''j''}} elements of sequence {{math|''B''}}.
* There are no common subsequences of length {{math|''k''}} for any fewer than {{math|''i''}} elements of sequence {{math|''A''}} or {{math|''j''}} elements of sequence {{math|''B''}}.

====Connecting {{math|''k''}}-candidates====
[[File:K Candidate Diagram.png|thumb|A diagram showing how using {{math|''k''}}-candidates reduces the amount of time and space needed to find the longest common subsequence of two sequences]]
To create the longest common subsequence from a collection of {{math|''k''}}-candidates, a grid with each sequence's contents on each axis is created. The {{math|''k''}}-candidates are marked on the grid. A common subsequence can be created by joining marked coordinates of the grid such that any increase in {{math|''i''}} is accompanied by an increase in&nbsp;{{math|''j''}}.

This is illustrated in the adjacent diagram. Black dots represent candidates that would have to be considered by the simple algorithm, and the black lines are connections that create common subsequences of length&nbsp;3. Red dots represent {{math|''k''}}-candidates that are considered by the Hunt–Szymanski algorithm, and the red line is the connection that creates a common subsequence of length&nbsp;3.
